author: Six questions from the former Module 3 bank, one per exam format, to try the app. Checked against GitHub Docs; not reviewed by an independent expert.

M3.title: Tooling, MCP, and Agent Execution Environments

units.U2: How agents interact with GitHub APIs and workflows
units.U3: MCP servers, registries, and allow lists

title: Sample · 6 questions, one per format

nuggets.title: The GitHub remote MCP server: HTTP type and one URL
nuggets.body:
In an IDE such as VS Code, you add the GitHub MCP server from Copilot Chat in Agent mode (Tools → Add MCP server). For the remote server you choose **HTTP** as the type, enter `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, choose the scope (this workspace or all workspaces) and authenticate with GitHub.

Remote is the recommended setup for most users. GitHub Enterprise Server supports only the local server.
nuggets.depth: Copilot cloud agent already has the GitHub MCP server enabled by default, with a token that has read-only access to the current repository. Reaching beyond that repository needs a token with broader access that you configure.
nuggets.watch: Remote = hosted URL + authentication. If an option pairs "remote GitHub MCP server" with a `localhost` address or a local command, it's wrong.

nuggets.title: A registry is a catalogue of MCP servers, with strict technical requirements
nuggets.example: With Azure API Center you enable anonymous access and enter only the base URL in the Copilot policy, without `/v0.1/servers`.
nuggets.watch: A registry makes servers discoverable. It doesn't block anything by itself; that's the allow list policy.

nuggets.title: The allow list policy: "Allow all" or "Registry only"
nuggets.body:
The allow list is a Copilot policy at organisation or enterprise level. First, **MCP servers in Copilot** must be enabled. Then **Restrict MCP access to registry servers** has two values:

- **Allow all**: developers can use any MCP server.
- **Registry only**: only servers listed in the configured registry.

Under Registry only, even local servers must be in the registry, and their server IDs must match exactly. The policy applies immediately, and it's tied to the organisation or enterprise that assigns the user's Copilot seat.
nuggets.example: Contoso lists four approved servers, one of them local, in its registry and selects Registry only. A developer's unlisted server stops working.
nuggets.depth: Enforcement happens in the clients (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Copilot CLI and others, from specific versions). **Copilot in the cloud isn't in the list of enforcing surfaces**: the cloud agent is governed by its repository MCP configuration. Enforcement matches server names/IDs, is in public preview and can be bypassed by editing config files; GitHub recommends `managed-settings.json` for stronger restriction. With several seats, an enterprise policy beats an organisation policy, and Registry only beats Allow all.
nuggets.watch: Setting a registry URL while leaving "Allow all" restricts nothing. And a local server that isn't in the registry is blocked under Registry only.

nuggets.title: Server, registry, allow list: three different jobs
nuggets.body:
The three MCP concepts solve different parts of one problem:

- The **server** exposes tools.
- The **registry** makes servers discoverable and standard to install.
- The **allow list** decides which servers are permitted.

Together they give agents more capabilities without the organisation losing control.
nuggets.example: Flow: the organisation publishes a registry and sets the policy → the developer's IDE discovers approved servers → the developer enables one → the agent uses its tools.
nuggets.watch: Questions often describe one need and offer all three as options. Ask: is this about *doing* (server), *finding* (registry) or *permitting* (allow list)?

nuggets.title: Permission boundaries: explicit and minimal
nuggets.body:
Permissions define what an agent can do inside its context. Workflows get them through tokens such as `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and they cover reading contents, writing code, creating pull requests and triggering workflows.

The rule: define permissions explicitly and keep them minimal.
nuggets.example: A nightly agent job that summarises changes and posts an issue comment needs `contents: read` and `issues: write`, and nothing else.
nuggets.depth: In `permissions:`, once you declare any scope, every scope you don't declare becomes `none`. Declare them at job level so only the job that needs a write permission has it.
nuggets.watch: `permissions: write-all`, or no `permissions:` key in a repository whose default is read and write, both break least privilege.

nuggets.title: Running an agent in CI: the workflow is the boundary
nuggets.body:
To run an agent as part of CI, you invoke it inside a workflow. The workflow fixes everything around it: the trigger (`workflow_dispatch`, `schedule`, `push`, `pull_request`), the `permissions:`, the runner, the checkout, the authentication, and the non-interactive command that runs the agent, optionally with a named custom agent.

The task runs on a defined runner, from a defined trigger, in one repository, with only the permissions granted to that workflow.
nuggets.example: A workflow on `schedule` checks out the repository and runs the agent with a prompt and no user interaction, with `permissions: contents: read`.
nuggets.watch: In CI nobody is there to approve a tool call. The limits must come from the workflow (permissions, secrets passed in), not from interactive prompts.

nuggets.skill: Operate agents with safe execution paths and robust error handling
nuggets.title: Rollback: isolation first, revert second
nuggets.body:
If an agent produces incorrect or unsafe changes, rollback keeps them out of the main codebase. Most of it comes for free from the way agents work: changes sit on a branch behind a pull request, so closing or discarding the pull request undoes everything.

If the change was already merged, revert the commits.
nuggets.example: A merged agent pull request breaks `main`. You open a revert pull request, let the required checks run, and merge it; the fix comes later in a new pull request.
nuggets.watch: Force-pushing the default branch back to an old commit is not the rollback path: it rewrites history and a ruleset normally blocks it. Use a revert through a pull request.

questions.stem:
A scheduled workflow runs an agent every night. The agent reads the repository's recent commits and posts a summary as a comment on a tracking issue. The repository's default workflow permissions are set to read and write.

You need to follow least privilege. Which configuration should you use for the job?

options.text: No `permissions:` key, so the job uses the repository default.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The default here is read and write for every scope.
Incorrect. It grants every scope at write level.
Incorrect. The job only reads code, so `contents: write` is more than it needs.
Correct. It can read the repository and comment on an issue; every other scope becomes `none`.

questions.explanation: Permissions should be explicit and minimal. Declaring scopes sets all undeclared ones to `none`.
questions.takeaway: Declare only the scopes the job uses; undeclared scopes become none.

evidence.quote: Permissions should always be explicitly defined and minimized.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: Adjust permissions based on what the workflow needs to do.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.note: When `permissions:` declares any scope, every scope that isn't declared is set to `none`.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

clues.text: Least-privilege tokens appear in M1, M2, M3 and M6.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: `GITHUB_TOKEN` scope and permissions blocks.

questions.stem:
An enterprise administrator hosts the company's MCP registry in Azure API Center and enters `https://contoso.data.eastus.azure-apicenter.ms/v0.1/servers` as the MCP Registry URL in the Copilot policy. Developers' IDEs show no servers from the registry.

Which two changes should the administrator make? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Enable anonymous access on the API Center registry.
options.rationale: Correct. Copilot must be able to fetch the registry without credentials.

options.text: Enter only the base URL of the API Center endpoint, without `/v0.1/servers`.
options.rationale: Correct. For Azure API Center the policy takes the base URL only.

options.text: Change the policy from "Registry only" to "Allow all".
options.rationale: Incorrect. That removes the restriction; it doesn't make the registry readable.

options.text: Add each developer's GitHub account as a reader on the API Center resource.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Copilot reads the registry anonymously, not as each developer.

options.text: Publish the registry over HTTP instead of HTTPS.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The registry endpoints must be served over HTTPS.

questions.explanation: Azure API Center can act as the MCP registry if anonymous access is enabled and the policy holds the base URL only.
questions.takeaway: Azure API Center registry: anonymous access + base URL only.

evidence.quote: Enable anonymous access so Copilot can fetch the registry
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: If using Azure API Center, enter the base URL only (do not include /v0.1/servers)
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

clues.text: M3 unit 3 gives the registry requirements as numbered steps, including the Azure API Center option.
Exact endpoints and the "base URL only" rule are precise, testable details.

questions.scenario:
This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals.

Fabrikam has an MCP registry that lists three approved remote servers. Developers also need one approved **local** MCP server that reads build logs.

**Goal:** developers must be able to use only approved MCP servers in their IDEs, including the local one.

items.solution: Enter the registry URL in the Copilot policy, select **Registry only**, and add the local server to the registry with a server ID that exactly matches the installed server.
items.explanation: Registry only limits developers to registry servers, and a local server is permitted when it's listed with a matching ID.

items.solution: Enter the registry URL in the Copilot policy and leave the restriction set to **Allow all**.
items.explanation: With Allow all, developers can add any server. The registry only helps discovery.

items.solution: Select **Registry only**, and tell developers to configure the local server by hand in their IDE because it doesn't need to be in the registry.
items.explanation: Under Registry only, local servers must also be in the registry, so the hand-configured server is blocked.

questions.takeaway: Registry only blocks everything not in the registry, local servers included; Allow all restricts nothing.

evidence.quote: If the Allow all option is selected, developers can add and use any MCP server without restrictions.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: If Registry only is selected, developers are limited to using only the MCP servers defined in the configured registry. In this case, even local MCP servers must be included in the registry, and their server IDs must match exactly.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

clues.text: M3 unit 3 Note: under Registry only, even local servers must be in the registry with matching IDs.
Local servers seem exempt from the policy.

questions.stem:
A pull request from an agent was reviewed and merged. An hour later you discover it broke the default branch, which is protected by a ruleset.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence to roll back safely and then get a corrected change?

items.text: Create a pull request that reverts the merged pull request.
Wait for the required checks to pass on the revert pull request.
Have the revert pull request reviewed and merge it.
Ask the agent for a corrected change in a new pull request.
Force-push the default branch back to the commit before the merge.
Add yourself to the ruleset bypass list to skip the checks.

questions.explanation: A merged change is rolled back by reverting its commits through the normal pull request path. Force-pushing rewrites history and is blocked by the ruleset, and bypassing checks removes the evidence you need.
questions.takeaway: Not merged → close the PR. Merged → revert through a PR, then fix in a new one.

evidence.quote: Closing or discarding the pull request
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: Reverting commits if changes are merged
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: Review all actions through pull requests
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

clues.text: Force-push and bypass lists are standard wrong options.

questions.stem:
You are explaining MCP governance to a new team.

Which component meets each need?

targets.text: Expose the ticketing system's operations as tools an agent can call.
targets.rationale: The server exposes tools and performs the real action.

targets.text: Let developers browse and install the company's approved servers from their IDE.
targets.rationale: The registry is the catalogue used for discovery and standard installation.

targets.text: Prevent developers from using any server the company hasn't approved.
targets.rationale: The allow list decides which servers are permitted.

questions.explanation: Server exposes, registry discovers, allow list permits. The firewall limits the cloud agent's network access and isn't part of this model.
questions.takeaway: Doing = server. Finding = registry. Permitting = allow list.

evidence.quote: Registry makes servers discoverable and trustable
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: Allow list decides which servers are permitted
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

clues.text: M3 unit 3 states the three roles in one list: server exposes, registry makes discoverable, allow list decides.

questions.stem:
You are adding the GitHub **remote** MCP server to a VS Code workspace so that Copilot's agent can use it.

How should you complete the configuration? Select the correct option for each box.

type.rationale: A remote server is reached over the network, so the type is HTTP. `stdio` and `local` start a process on your machine.

url.rationale: This is the hosted GitHub MCP server. `localhost` would be a local server, and `/v0.1/servers` is a registry endpoint, not a server.

questions.explanation: The remote GitHub MCP server is added as an HTTP server at `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, then you authenticate with GitHub.
questions.takeaway: Remote GitHub MCP server = type HTTP + api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ + sign in.

evidence.quote: Select HTTP as the server type
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: Enter the server URL (example for GitHub MCP server):
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn

evidence.quote: A remote MCP server is hosted elsewhere and accessed over the network.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn
